items.title: The next developer interface is ambient intelligence
items.lede: AI, agents, voice, and physical controls are shifting software development from operating tools to expressing intent—and helping developers stay focused on building.
items.text:
For most of my career, building software started with the same setup: keyboard, mouse, editor, terminal, browser, and an impressive number of tabs I was definitely going to look at later. The tools changed, but the relationship did not. Like most developers, I learned commands, memorized shortcuts, and adapted my thinking to the machine.

AI is changing that relationship and not because I can prompt my way to some workable code. It’s more because the system behind it can understand a repository, choose the right model, plan work, use tools, edit files, run commands, inspect failures, and keep going within boundaries the developer controls.

We’ve made it possible for a developer to describe an outcome, and GitHub Copilot can gather repository context, inspect symbols and dependencies, edit files, run tests, and revise the implementation. In the IDE, agent mode keeps that loop interactive. GitHub Copilot coding agent can take an issue into an isolated GitHub Actions-powered environment and return a pull request for review. This is not just faster coding. It is the shift from issuing commands to making intent executable. The developer still owns the outcome, but the work looks subtly different.

AI-assisted development compresses that chain of events. We spend less time navigating tools and more time setting direction, supplying context, defining constraints, and reviewing evidence. The development workflow now is about understanding the structure of codebases, the customer, and what a good solution should feel like.

This makes developers’ jobs even more important, and their time more valuable. It makes judgment more valuable. It makes taste more valuable. An agent can generate three implementations before you finish your tea, but someone still has to decide whether the abstraction belongs, the migration is safe, the tests prove anything useful, and the result solves the problem.

That is the most important change in the craft: the developer remains accountable for the outcome, even as more mechanics are delegated.

So what does this mean for the emerging developer workflow? The goal is to embed AI into the workflow, not beside it. It’s more of an ambient intelligence.

That requires portable context. MCP connects agents to tools and services; repository instructions and skills encode conventions; hooks enforce policy and validate output. Simpler interfaces need explicit context underneath.

I see three layers: modality captures intent; the harness plans and acts; the control plane lets developers inspect, redirect, and approve. The best products connect all three without surrendering control.

Together, they let developers move across text, voice, and physical controls without losing context.

Why physical controls are interesting again

I, and many others in the maker community, have been experimenting with ambient control devices, from inexpensive hackable picture frames to ESP32 devices with screens attached. Agentic coding is past just a keyboard and a terminal into alternative interfaces.

Getting this kind of technology into everyone’s hands is something that I’m very passionate about and so over the past 18 months we’ve been working with Logitech on their MX Keypad and how it can help this new way of working.

The Logitech MX Keypad turns familiar developer actions into programmable inputs to accelerate workflows that are ambient and contextual to the work devs are doing. In GitHub Copilot app, a key can submit a parameterized prompt, open or resume a Copilot session, invoke an IDE command, or trigger a multi-step sequence. The hardware earns its place only when that shortcut removes enough friction to keep you in the code, but still gives you control.

Physical controls work when an action repeats often enough that removing a few steps preserves concentration. Not every developer needs another device on the desk, and not every interruption deserves a key. However, with this experience the developer decides which actions earn that shortcut and when the keyboard, command palette, or voice is better. Maintaining flow is the key, and a good interface gives some of that attention back.

GUIs made software visual.

items.title: How to continue a GitHub Copilot app session in VS Code
items.lede: Learn how to move an agent session from the GitHub Copilot app into VS Code without losing the conversation, code changes, or working context.
items.text:
The agent has finished the bulk of your change. Now you want to inspect one implementation detail, adjust a few lines by hand, and run the project locally before you ship it.

But the work is sitting in the GitHub Copilot app… and your editor is where you review diffs, debug code, and make final adjustments. Do you have to choose between staying in the session and starting over in Visual Studio Code?

You don’t. You can open the Copilot app session directly in VS Code and continue with its conversation, code changes, and working context intact. That means Copilot can handle the repetitive or time-consuming work, then hand control back to you for closer review, hands-on editing, and local testing.

In this tutorial, you’ll learn how to:

- Open a Copilot app session in VS Code.

- Review the agent’s changes line by line.

- Continue the same conversation from your editor.

- Modify and test the code locally.

- Push your updates to the pull request associated with the session.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you have:

- The GitHub Copilot app installed and signed in.

- Visual Studio Code installed and connected to the same GitHub account.

- A Copilot app session with code changes you want to review or continue.

- Permission to work in and push changes to the session’s repository.

This tutorial assumes you are already comfortable navigating VS Code, running commands in its integrated terminal, and working with Git branches and pull requests.

1. Start with a session in the Copilot app

Open the session you want to continue. Before handing it off, take a moment to review the task and the work Copilot completed.

A session contains more than a collection of modified files. It also records the task, the plan, and the conversation that produced those changes. That context is important when you want to understand why Copilot chose a particular implementation or ask it to revise part of the work.

You do not need to summarize that history or copy it into a new chat before moving to VS Code.

2. Open the session in VS Code

From the session, select Open in VS Code. If the app presents more than one supported editor or VS Code installation, choose the one you want to use.

VS Code opens the project using the worktree associated with the session. It also displays the existing session in the Copilot sidebar.

That gives you three connected pieces of the original work:

- The session context: The task, plan, and conversation remain available.

- The diff: The files and lines changed by the agent are ready for review.

- The worktree: VS Code opens the same isolated working tree the session used.

You are continuing the existing session, not reconstructing it in a new editor window.

3. Review the agent’s changes

Before editing, inspect the diff in VS Code. Open the Source Control view to see the changed files, then select a file to review its changes line by line.

Review the implementation as you would any other proposed change. In particular, check that:

- The code solves the requested problem.

- The implementation follows the repository’s conventions.

- Error states and edge cases are handled appropriately.

- Tests cover the behavior that changed.

- No unrelated files or behaviors were modified.

The preserved conversation can help explain how Copilot arrived at the implementation. If something is unclear, continue prompting Copilot in the sidebar. For example:

Explain why you changed this function instead of adding a new helper. Identify any behavior this could affect.

You can also ask Copilot to make another change. Because the session and worktree remain connected, you do not have to describe the task from the beginning.

4. Make a hands-on edit

Once you understand the proposed changes, edit any file directly in VS Code.

This is useful for adjustments that are faster or easier to make by hand, such as:

- Refining a label or error message.

- Renaming a variable for clarity.

- Adjusting layout or styling.

- Adding a missing test case.

- Applying a repository-specific convention.

You are editing the session’s existing worktree, so your manual changes build directly on the agent’s work.

items.title: How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity
items.lede: Three Java Champions share how they use GitHub Copilot to solve problems, accelerate development, and keep humans responsible for the results.
items.text:
AI coding tools can generate code quickly, but speed alone does not solve the hardest software engineering problems. Developers still need to provide context, validate results, protect maintainability, and remain accountable for what ships.

To learn how experienced developers strike that balance, we spoke with three Java Champions, all with over a decade of experience in using Java. They shared concrete examples of using GitHub Copilot in production and open source, along with the practices they use to turn AI-generated output into reliable software.

Here are the tips they shared with us.

Meet the Java Champions

- Vlad Mihalcea, founder of Hypersistence and author of the book High-Performance Java Persistence

- Patrick Baumgartner, software crafter at 42talents with 20+ years of Java experience

- Frank Delporte, senior technical writer at Azul and maintainer of Foojay.io with 15+ years of Java experience

Vlad Mihalcea

GitHub profile: @vladmihalcea

How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently?

I’ve been using it to analyze, design, and implement various features in both Hypersistence Utils and Hypersistence Optimizer.

For example, I’ve been wanting for a long time to develop a web application that provides Optimizer event history so we can see how performance improvement efforts are materializing in application performance. Before AI, I kept postponing this task because it would have taken me weeks to develop. But using Copilot is like having a new team member, so I used it to create an app that will ship in the next version of Hypersistence Optimizer. Instead of weeks, this task took just two days to implement.

What’s your typical usage? Are you using GitHub Copilot as an IDE plugin or the GitHub Copilot app?

I use GitHub Copilot in IntelliJ IDEA because it’s convenient to run while reviewing source code or during a debug session.

It’s very useful as a code assistant, and it helps me speed up both investigations and building prototypes for features that need validation.

I still review the plans and the code that is generated by AI since their goal is to improve my productivity, not replace me entirely. While AI provides the right answer in many situations, there are still times when the response is not satisfactory and requires my intervention.

Can you share some tips and best practices? For example, which skills are you using?

I created my own skills so that whatever text Copilot generates looks like something I wrote by hand.

This skill captures my voice from 65 of my published articles, so a draft comes back sounding like my blog instead of like a language model. This is really useful when generating documentation for this project, since it lets the LLM learn from 12 years of blogging and provide examples that follow the same principles, such as expressiveness, testability, and simplicity.

Throughout my career as a software engineer, I’ve learned that we spend far more time on code maintenance than on creating it. Therefore, because maintenance and stability are critical for existing products, I developed skills that help AI mimic existing code practices in accordance with the principle of least astonishment.

One tip is to change the model type based on the type of operation. For thorough thinking, I use Opus with the 1 million context window and Extra High or Max reasoning. However, for simpler tasks, such as generating reports, release notes, or verifying documentation, I use lighter models that consume fewer tokens.

Patrick Baumgartner

GitHub profile: @patbaumgartner

Your work involves coaching teams. What is your approach?

A lot of my work happens while the normal business still has to keep running. You cannot stop everything for six months to “transform.” We usually start by solving immediate problems together, understand where the team currently stands, define where we want to go and how we will know that we are improving, and then move there step by step.

items.title: The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure
items.lede: We moved a copy of 99.99999% of GitHub’s repositories to Azure. Here’s how per-reference quorums will bring over the rest, and how object storage lets reads scale independently.
items.text:
Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. The rest are among the busiest on the platform, and they’re held back by just one thing: a 25ms round trip.

In an earlier blog post, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture:

- Minimize coordination

- Decouple storage from compute

In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own.

How we got here

The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. At the beginning of our migration, the remaining capacity with all possible expansion gave us enough time to migrate safely, but not enough to do it slowly.

While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. Given our scale and how critical the service is to the community, we needed to sequence the work carefully: move the data first, then evolve the architecture once it arrived.

Git operations are a Tier 0 service: they’re a core function of GitHub, and nearly everything in GitHub depends on the repository data. That meant the data, services, and every dependency had to move first. The first copy of a repository landed in Azure’s Central US region in August 2025. Today, most repositories have two of their five replicas in Azure, and Azure serves about half of Git traffic. For most of that time, Azure absorbed our growth while our own data centers held steady.

During the migration, traffic follows the data. Most repositories have five replicas to balance durability, availability, and scale. To minimize read latency, Spokes uses preferential routing to direct traffic to a replica in the same region and availability zone as the request. As replicas move to Azure, the share of the traffic that can be served from Azure grows with each one, until the last replica arrives and the old region stops receiving requests entirely. Every repository goes through this process:

No repository left behind

So, what about the remaining 0.00001% of repositories?

In our current architecture, a repository hosted in more than one region has a lower write throughput ceiling. Spokes’ quorum only needs a majority to commit a write, but it waits for every healthy replica to respond (up to a timeout) before moving on, so slow replicas delay every write rather than falling behind. In practice, that means the slowest healthy replica sets the latency of every write, and because each write holds a repository-wide lock until it commits, it also sets the throughput ceiling. Once a replica lives in the target Azure region, it’s about 1,000 miles from our data centers, making each network round trip around 25ms, and a write requires multiple round trips. A repository already near its throughput ceiling can’t absorb that on every serialized write; it would fall further behind with every push.

This is where our first principle, minimizing coordination, comes into play. Specifically for this case: don’t serialize what doesn’t need to be. Git’s consistency requirements apply to each reference individually. Once the server accepts an update to a reference, no client should see an older value afterward, only that value or a newer one. That holds whether the update is a fast-forward, a force push, or a delete. But in most cases, updates to different references don’t depend on each other and can be applied independently.

So, we’re changing the scope of the quorum from the whole repository to individual references.

items.title: How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills
items.lede: As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team spotlights @r31n, diving into their research approach, favorite bug classes, and advice for aspiring hackers.
items.text:
As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight another top-performing security researcher from the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @r31n!

As home to the world’s developers, GitHub is dedicated to the security and reliability of the code behind millions of projects, and our Bug Bounty Program remains a cornerstone of that commitment. Collaboration with external researchers is one of the most effective ways to improve security, and every year, the community helps us identify and fix vulnerabilities that make the platform safer for everyone.

The security research landscape is changing rapidly. AI has lowered the barrier to entry and become a genuine force multiplier. We use it across our own internal security programs, and we welcome researchers who do the same. However, what separates great research has not changed: validation, a working proof of concept, and a clear demonstration of real security impact. The tools do not matter; the quality of the work does. The researchers we spotlight this month exemplify exactly that standard through findings that are verified, reproducible, and demonstrate that a security boundary has been crossed rather than simply theorizing that one exists.

Researchers who consistently work at that level can earn an invitation to our permanent VIP program, which offers higher payouts, faster response times, and early previews of beta products and features. Learn more about how to qualify on our public bounty site.

As we wrap up our Cybersecurity Awareness Month celebration, we interview @r31n, a researcher renowned for their work on GitHub Enterprise Server, where they have repeatedly uncovered high-impact issues. Their reports consistently include working proofs of concept and clear reproduction steps, helping our engineering teams move from triage to remediation more quickly.

How did you get started in security and bug bounty, and what keeps you coming back to GitHub’s program?

I got into bug bounty because I wanted a way to keep developing my security skills outside the environments I work with every day. It exposes me to different products, technologies, and architectures I probably wouldn’t run into otherwise. GitHub is one of those programs I keep coming back to because there’s just so much surface area. It’s large, complex, and constantly changing. New features ship all the time, so it never really feels like a finished target. They also work closely with researchers, the bounty structure is competitive, and the swag is a nice bonus. It’s simply a program I enjoy spending time on.

What are your favorite classes of bugs to research and why?

I don’t really have one favorite bug class. What interests me more are exploit chains, especially cases where a few things that seem relatively harmless on their own come together and create something much more serious. An open redirect is a simple example. By itself, the impact might be limited. But if you find an allowlisted-domain SSRF that follows redirects, suddenly that open redirect can become a useful part of a much bigger chain. That’s probably the part of vulnerability research I enjoy most: finding those connections, looking at two or three separate bugs and realizing they can be combined in a way that wasn’t intended. It takes some technical knowledge, but also quite a bit of creativity.

How do you keep your skills sharp and stay on top of new vulnerability trends?

It’s actually a mix of different things. Security blogs, vulnerability write-ups, conference talks, proof of concepts, research papers, courses. I try to learn from wherever useful work is being shared. But most of it only really sticks once I try it myself. I can read a vulnerability write-up, but working through it myself gives me a much deeper understanding. If I actually reproduce the technique, play around with it, break it, and figure out why it behaves the way it does, that’s when it really stays with me. And later, when I see a similar pattern on a real target, it’s much easier to recognize.

What tools or workflows have been gamechangers for your research? Any lesser-known utilities you’d recommend?

items.title: Octoverse: Commits, pushes, reach new highs in 2026 as developers build with agents
items.lede: See how a record year of growth reached every industry, every field, and every kind of builder in the 2026 Octoverse report.
items.text:
Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than in 2024 and 2025 combined.

Behind that number are developers building what interests them and what their communities need. In Nepal, one developer built a flood bulletin on GitHub Pages with verified information on roads, rescue, weather, and power. It has since grown into Gati, a Nepali-first relay of official disaster alerts that runs on GitHub Pages and Actions. Elsewhere, developers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory are creating software designed to run programs aboard spacecraft, and fans built open-source firmware that lets people customize their e-readers. Curiosity, aimed in every direction, at a scale GitHub hasn’t seen before.

That growth happened quickly. Partway through the year, activity on GitHub bent sharply upward, just as agents went from something developers were trying out to something they were working alongside. Developers picked from more models than ever and built in industries we are highlighting in this report for the first time, from health care to agriculture.

Octoverse is our chance to step back and look at the whole picture. This year, that picture is bigger than ever. Here is what stood out most:

- More AI, more of everything. Among repositories created this year, the average repo with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as the average new repo without one.

- As of September, developers start more than 40% of pull requests with an agent. In March, it was 17%. For a growing share of work, the first move is now directing an agent, and review is how developers shape what comes back.

- Developers move fast on model choice. In September, 61% of GitHub Copilot users used more than one model, and requests spread across general purpose, deep reasoning and planning, and fast and lightweight models

- Builders are showing up from every field. This year, for the first time, we’re sharing our view of public repositories by industry. Repos serving mining, construction, health care, and agriculture have each grown several times over since 2022.

Underneath it all, AI models and the harnesses built around them have advanced over the past year, and developers have more to choose from. Growth is moving quickly: one year into last year’s five-year developer growth projections, every country we projected has already closed at least a fifth of its distance to 2030, and our own forecasting models no longer agree on where it will go next.

The year developers set a new pace

This year was all about momentum. Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day.

Agents were one of the tools developers leaned on hardest this year, pulling them deeper into daily work. Among repos created this year, the average repo with an agent configuration file logged eight times as many commits as the average new repo without one, sign that individuals and teams building with agents from day one are moving at a markedly different pace.

Developers also relied on automations to keep projects moving. GitHub Actions ran a job 1,440 times every second this year. This equals 124 million times a day and is more than three times last year’s total. Developers merged more than 30 million Dependabot pull requests to keep dependencies current and reduce the use of known vulnerabilities, about double 2025’s pace.

Our telemetry shows activity climbing steadily from January, then surging around June, as if developers everywhere saw new possibilities at once. Right around then, a cluster of industry-wide shifts landed: better underlying models, the harnesses and tools built around them, and the agents running on both. Agents moved from single-session tools to persistent ones that could track progress across days and orchestrate other specialized agents.

items.title: GitHub Universe 2026: Evolving every layer of the stack
items.lede: Today, we laid out our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive, end-to-end software delivery system in the world.
items.text:
Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters.

Today at GitHub Universe, we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it.

Our vision: From idea to completed software

The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better.

This agentic software delivery system solves for three things:

- Velocity: get from idea to completed software as quickly, efficiently, and cost-effectively as possible

- Intelligence: combine context across the platform with a continuous learning engine, so the system gets better as you use it

- Quality: make completed work secure by default and catch bugs before they ship

GitHub is built for developers and their agents. We’re also making the underlying primitives available, so you can build your own bespoke solutions. You stay in control of the work, the tools, and the cost.

New features and products that move the work forward

Today at Universe, we showed some of the latest products and features in action, starting with the GitHub Copilot app.

GitHub Copilot app: From issue to merge, in one app

The GitHub Copilot app is designed from the ground up for agentic software delivery. It connects your agents and tools across projects, so you can direct the work without making every handoff. And it’s for more than producing code: you can write specs, present design discussions, or analyze telemetry in one agent-first surface.

Copilot Fusion: Multi-model orchestration at its finest

Different tasks need different models. Developers shouldn’t have to manage every model choice to get the right result at the right price. Copilot Fusion evaluates what a task needs across reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool use, then chooses how to execute across one or more models. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Fusion Max scored within two points of Opus 5.5 Max at half the cost and 40% less time per task.

Copilot projects: Give Copilot a goal

Available natively in the GitHub Copilot app starting today, Copilot projects let you run agent work across multiple repos in fully managed, parallel sessions. You have one place to track progress, make decisions, and direct what happens next. That means you can spend less time managing execution and more time deciding what’s worth building.

Session continuity: Keep working across surfaces

Your work shouldn’t restart when you switch devices or tools. Session continuity lets you start and follow the same cloud agent session across the GitHub app, VS Code, the CLI, and the web. Start from your phone at standup, steer it from VS Code at your desk, and check in on it from github.com at lunch. The agent keeps working in the cloud. Our multi-model harness that enables it is powerful, fast, and cost-efficient.

Copilot automations: Learning from the results

Copilot automations let you create AI-powered workflows within your repo. They run in the cloud, and you can kick them off manually or set them up to respond to an event or run on a schedule. That lets you coordinate agents to handle tasks such as issue triage and code review. And now, automations can learn from their outcomes and propose improvements for you to review and approve. That’s the learning engine in practice. Use the results of the completed work to make the next run better.

items.title: Game Off 2026: The theme is SHIFT
items.lede: GitHub’s annual month-long game jam is back for its 14th year! This November, make a game inspired by the theme SHIFT. Change gears, swap perspectives, bend reality, or just press a certain key.
items.text:
It’s time to make Shift happen.

Game Off, GitHub’s annual month-long game jam, returns for its 14th year this November. Thousands of developers have joined us over the years to make everything from polished platformers to wonderfully weird experiments.

Whether you’re making your first game or your fiftieth, we’d love for you to join us.

The theme for Game Off 2026 is SHIFT!

Shift gears. Shift perspectives. Shift dimensions. Shift bits. Work the night shift. Or make a game where the only buttons are the Shift keys.

How you interpret the theme is entirely up to you.

You have until December 1, 2026, at 13:37 PST to build and submit a game inspired by SHIFT. Strong or loose inspirations apply!

Join Game Off 2026 on itch.io

shift /ʃɪft/

Noun

- A change in position, direction, perspective, or reality.

- A period of scheduled work, usually when something breaks.

- A keyboard key used to capitalize letters, sprint in games, and accidentally enable sticky keys.

- In computing, an operation that moves bits left or right, because apparently bits need exercise too.

Verb

- To change gears, direction, or the laws of physics.

- To move between worlds, dimensions, timelines, or questionable life choices.

- To transform into something (or someone) entirely different.

- To pass responsibility to somebody else, especially when the production build breaks.

Acronyms (that we definitely just made up)

Okay, we made these up:

- Space Hamsters Initiating Faster Travel

- Shapeshifters Hiding In Forgotten Temples

- Suspicious Humans Investigating Feral Toasters

- Skeletons Hastily Improvising Functional Transportation

Or invent your own. We love seeing where you take the theme.

Need inspiration? Here are a few concept ideas

- A one-button (or two-button) game where the Shift keys are is your only control.

- A racing game where shifting gears changes more than your speed. Second gear reverses gravity, third slows time, and fourth removes the brakes.

- A perspective puzzler where rotating the camera turns walls into floors and shifts shadows into platforms.

- A puzzle-platformer where you shift between two overlapping realities. That broken bridge might exist in the other world. Unfortunately, so might the monster standing on it.

- A shapeshifting adventure where you transform into creatures and objects, inheriting their abilities and weaknesses.

- A night-shift horror game set in a convenience store where the customers get progressively stranger, and whatever’s in aisle seven definitely isn’t covered by your training.

- A comedy detective game where you committed the crime and must shift the blame onto increasingly unlikely suspects without contradicting the evidence.

- A programming puzzler: Use bitwise shifts to manipulate the world. Shift left to double an object’s size, shift right to halve it, and discover what happens when you run out of bits.

- An adventure game about convincing somebody to cover your shift so you can attend the final boss battle.

Of course, you could also build a game about shifting tectonic plates, shape-shifting aliens, shifting alliances, shifting sands, or a particularly ambitious stick shift.

Don’t overthink it. Pick an interpretation that interests you and see where it takes you.

Pro tip: Start with one mechanic and one playable level. Get those working before adding the multiverse. Future you (and your bug tracker) will thank you.

Need another perspective? Try brainstorming with GitHub Copilot. Give it the theme, a few constraints, and see what it comes up with:

Act as an indie game designer. Suggest 10 original game concepts inspired by SHIFT, each with a unique core mechanic, genre, and technical twist. Prioritize ideas a solo developer could prototype in a weekend.

How to participate

Work alone or form a team. Use whichever programming languages, game engines, frameworks, libraries, and tools make sense for your game.

- Create a free GitHub account if you don’t already have one.

- Join the jam. Head to the Game Off 2026 page on itch.io. If you don’t have an itch.io account, you can sign in with your GitHub account.

- Create a public repository.

items.title: Arnis turns any place on Earth into a Minecraft world
items.lede: Louis Erbkamm built the first prototype in his free time. Now GitHub Copilot helps him maintain it alone.
items.text:
Louis Erbkamm knows his way around Arnis, the smallest town in Germany, but he’s never set foot in it.

I know where the shops are. Where the boats are… I know the city pretty well, but I haven’t been there yet.

Louis Erbkamm, maintainer of Arnis

Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors.

Two weeks and a slow prototype

Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school.

That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow.

Arnis has a lot of buildings, it has streets, it has waters, it has all kinds of different elements that are useful to test with.

Louis

The project didn’t have a name yet, so it borrowed the town’s unique moniker.

A community that brings its own ideas

When Arnis added elevation, its worlds stopped being flat, and geospatial specialists from all over showed up with ideas on how best to integrate it. They started discussions on their own, and Louis says that’s exactly what he needed.

Bigger calls happen in the open too: before porting Arnis from Python to Rust, Louis opened discussions on GitHub to hear different perspectives. Contributors have since translated Arnis into about 20 languages and built major features of their own.

The best thing that has happened to me is essentially this big community on GitHub to see actually people from all kinds of different fields coming together to work on something that I started as a side project.

Louis

How a trash bin gets into Minecraft

Some features start on a walk. Louis noticed how many trash bins there were in his city, and there were none in his generated worlds.

Minecraft has no dedicated bins, so he took the question to the community, and together they found a block that fit. Placing one follows the same path as everything else: for the area a user selects, Arnis queries OpenStreetMap for every mapped element, then looks up each element’s coordinates and type.

If an element isn’t mapped, Arnis can’t place it. For structures too detailed for the map to describe, like the Statue of Liberty in New York, or Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro, Arnis converts 3D models into Minecraft blocks.

One maintainer, a stack of pull requests

As the sole maintainer, Louis reviews every pull request himself, and they stack up. He usually spends evenings or weekends working on Arnis, which means the community has to wait for him to be done with work for the day.

He uses GitHub Copilot to get an overview of open issues and bugs from the latest release, see how many people are running into them, trace where a bug came from in the codebase, and create a fix. Since he brought AI into the project, he says, code reviews and documentation have both increased.

I could delegate those annoying and boring tasks to Copilot, while I could still have a look at those really cool topics that are related to the development of it.

Louis

Sub-agents that look for regressions

Big features arrive as big pull requests.

Louis opens a large pull request in the GitHub Copilot app for a first overview and a performance review, with Copilot running in the background looking for small changes that would cut memory usage or generation time.

It takes just one wrong calculation in street lights, for example, to make the generation time of an entire city much slower.

Louis

He also keeps a mental list of the areas of the codebase that need extra care whenever someone changes them, and he has written the same warnings out by hand over and over.

items.title: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture
items.lede: GitHub’s new Git storage architecture is built so thousands of agents can push to a single repository at once. Here’s how it works.
items.text:
Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running.

Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post, we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage.

We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.

The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components.

Building for agent scale

We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes:

- Horizontal scale is how many developers and agents can work across many repositories. Many of GitHub’s current approaches on this axis have been battle-tested over the years and are carried forward to the new architecture: partitioning of tenants across infrastructure, isolation and/or fairness enforcement of tenant traffic, and load-aware routing, to name a few.

- Vertical scale is how many developers and agents can work on one repository. As agents write more code, we expect individual repositories to get larger and busier, so most of our requirements came from the vertical axis.

Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes.

We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then.

We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to:

- Accept thousands of writes per second.

- Support multiple writer nodes. There are two reasons for this:

- Experience has taught us that indexing incoming packs and checking object connectivity are the most CPU-expensive parts of a write, and that cost scales with the size of the write, so a single node will become compute-bound quickly.

- Spreading that work across many nodes improves fault tolerance and shortens recovery when a node fails.

items.title: Accessibility statements now have a home on GitHub
items.lede: GitHub now highlights ACCESSIBILITY.md files and helps maintainers document accessibility goals, known barriers, supported environments, contributor expectations, and reporting processes.
items.text:
Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change.

An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers.

GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find

GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document.

GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works:

- Contribution guidelines explain how to propose changes

- Codes of conduct establish expectations for participation

- Security policies explain how to report vulnerabilities

Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance.

New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. The statement explains how to report a barrier and what to expect next, while the label helps maintainers organize and track the resulting work.

Accessibility statements make project practices visible

GitHub CLI’s accessibility statement, for example, documents settings, known barriers, and workarounds. It explains why table output can be difficult to follow with a screen reader and provides a command that prints pull request numbers and titles one per line instead. It also asks contributors changing prompts or output to show the results with relevant accessibility settings enabled. Developers using the CLI get a specific workaround; developers contributing to it get clear expectations for their changes.

The GitHub Annotation Toolkit’s accessibility statement documents a limitation of its Figma library: annotations use canvas position, connecting lines, and matching numbers to visually convey relationships. Access to individual canvas objects does not necessarily communicate what those relationships are.

The statement gives collaborators a concrete alternative: provide a structured text description that identifies each annotated element, its intended semantics and behavior, and any relevant ordering. For developers preparing or receiving a design handoff, this explains what information needs to accompany the visual annotations.

The file also explains how to report accessibility barriers and explicitly states that the library has not undergone keyboard-only or screen-reader testing. Readers get both practical guidance and clear limits on what the project has verified. Showing this information in the repository overview makes it easier to find alongside the project’s other documentation.

Document what the project can maintain

There is no one fixed format for an ACCESSIBILITY.md file. A small library, command-line tool, documentation site, and large web application have different users, risks, and maintenance capacity. Start with accurate information that the project can keep current.

- Priorities and goals: Explain why accessibility matters to the project and which user experiences receive attention.

- Contributor expectations: Describe the accessibility checks, evidence, or review practices expected for changes, including instructions for human contributors and coding agents.

- Reporting accessibility barriers: Provide a direct, accessible reporting path. Do not require disability disclosure, screenshots, or recordings.

- Response process: Explain how maintainers acknowledge, triage, track, and communicate about accessibility issues. If the project uses severity levels, let maintainers assign or confirm them during triage.

- Supported environments: List the platforms, browsers, input methods, and assistive technologies the project supports or has tested.

items.title: Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering
items.lede: Writing code got faster. The work around it didn’t. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment.
items.text:
This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?

Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.

As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.

Plan: Get everyone and every agent on the same page

See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.

You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan.

- Plan together where your team already works. Use Copilot in Slack or Teams to collaborate with everyone involved—from product managers and designers to analysts and business stakeholders. Bring in context from connected tools so your team can check assumptions, contribute ideas, and refine requirements together.

- Turn agreed-upon requirements into actionable work. Ask Copilot to create GitHub Issues with the context and acceptance criteria needed for implementation, breaking out tasks that can be handled separately.

- Keep routine triage from consuming planning time. Use GitHub Agentic Workflows to label your issues and estimate task complexity. Assign low-complexity tasks directly to Copilot, then spend your time focusing on harder decisions.

- Give complex work the planning it needs. Use Plan Mode in your preferred Copilot surface to compare approaches and refine an implementation plan. Review and approve the plan before handing it off to Copilot to begin implementation.

What took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable plan, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped issues, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.

Build: Move more than one task forward at a time

You’re ready to turn that plan into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.

You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.

- Continue your conversation from another device. Session continuity lets you pick up the same Copilot session across clients, so you can work wherever it’s most convenient for you.

- Let work continue after you close your laptop. Copilot runs tasks in cloud sandboxes, keeping execution off your machine and allowing you to leave and return to a session later.

- Work on separate tasks without mixing their edits. The Copilot app gives sessions isolated copies of the repository, so an implementation task and a documentation update don’t share an unfinished working tree.

- Carry project knowledge into each task.

items.title: Git security vulnerabilities announced
items.lede: Git is releasing updates addressing six security vulnerabilities affecting clones, reference handling, merges, binary patches, and imports. Here is what users need to know.
items.text:
Editor’s note (November 17, 2026): This post has been updated with additional CVE information and updated guidance for GitHub Enterprise Server users. Please see the release information below for the versions that include the fixes.

Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Vulnerabilities in Git

CVE-2026-111760: Code execution when cloning malicious repositories

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.

An attacker-controlled Git server can exploit this discrepancy to replace a clone’s .git file or directory, redirecting Git to attacker-controlled configuration or hooks.

For recursive clones, this can execute attacker-controlled code during the clone. For non-recursive clones, an attacker can replace the top-level .git directory with a file pointing to attacker-controlled repository metadata. The clone can then report an error and recommend running git status in the resulting directory; following that advice can execute attacker-controlled code.

The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114469: Out-of-bounds reads when applying binary patches

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-105437: Heap corruption during large merges

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

items.title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
items.lede: Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them.
items.text:
How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline.

An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database.

I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills”.

Define one job and when it applies

A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With Proof Agent, we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose:

---
name: proof-agent
description: Adversarial verification of AI-generated work. Spawns an independent verifier to check for false claims, broken code, and security issues.
---

At the center is a simple rule: self-verification is not verification.

The When to Verify section in Proof Agent’s SKILL.md says when to invoke the skill. The remaining instructions explain what the verifier reviews and what evidence to include in its findings.

Coordinate multiple skills for a larger workflow

When the judgment that makes a data pipeline correct lives in four different people’s heads, those four people are the roadmap. Each change to the pipeline depends on their availability and knowledge of the data. Data Forge is an example of how to capture parts of that judgment in skills that work together.

In the support-desk pipeline example, we start with a request for metrics that count incidents created and resolved. Before building the pipeline, the forge-init skill discovers details such as source tables and naming conventions, then writes them to a resolved manifest. The other skills read that manifest for the project context they need.

The forge-builder skill then coordinates the work from the issue through to a pull request. It uses forge-dbx to query the data platform and forge-lint to apply the team’s standards as it designs and builds the pipeline. A person reviews the proposed decisions along the way, and the resulting pull request contains the pipeline code, schema changes, and tests.

Each skill has a defined responsibility, and they share project context instead of rediscovering it independently. When a step changes, you can change one skill and leave the rest alone.

Skills fit bounded, repeatable work that benefits from reusable judgment, such as a checklist, release, migration, or metric pipeline. If a workflow needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail, long-running control, or permissions enforced outside the model, an application is a better fit.

Keep project configuration out of the skill

We don’t want to hardcode every project’s names, database, or conventions into the skills. In the Data Forge support-desk example, a manifest describes the project, metric store, and platform so the skills can use the right project details without baking them into their instructions:

project:
name: "support-desk"
store_name: "support_metric_store"

platform:
engine: "duckdb"
pipeline_framework: "spark_python"
duckdb_dir: "warehouse"

With the discovered details in the resolved manifest, the other skills don’t have to make their own assumptions about the project.

Keep discovered project details separate from team standards.

items.title: GitHub availability report: October 2026
items.lede: In October, we experienced eight incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services.
items.text:
We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

October 05 19:11 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 38 minutes)

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

What went wrong and why?

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How did we respond?

- A partial networking failure began, and actions jobs started backing up.

items.title: Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.
items.lede: In the Codename MDASH pilot, GitHub and Microsoft turned thousands of raw AI findings into 99 checked, private reports with suggested fixes for six widely used open source projects. Maintainers have already fixed more than half.
items.text:
AI has made finding potential vulnerabilities fast and cheap. Fixing them still takes human judgment, and in open source, that work falls to maintainers. Many are already flooded with AI-generated security findings, including duplicates and reports that aren’t vulnerabilities at all. Another raw scan doesn’t help them. Anyone pointing a new model at a project should ask its maintainers first and come with fixes, not just findings.

Maintainers are under intense pressure from this flood of reports. As Christian Grobmeier, a maintainer of Log4j, has put it, the AI defending open source has to be better than the AI attacking it.

AI shouldn’t add to maintainers’ workload. So, with maintainers, GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot together: could AI help maintainers ship fixes instead of handing them more findings?

GitHub and Microsoft are using Codename MDASH, Microsoft’s multi-model agentic scanning harness, to find and fix security vulnerabilities in widely used open source software, strengthening the foundation that much of the world’s code is built on.

The process

Our pilot had two goals: send only findings that matter, and never send a maintainer an unverified finding. Here’s how it worked:

- Find. Codename MDASH, an AI system from Microsoft Security, scanned each project using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model and suggested fixes for what it found.

- Filter. An AI triage agent from the GitHub Security Lab, built on tailored Copilot skills, removed duplicates, checked validity, and focused on high-impact bugs, so maintainers never had to review raw scan results.

- Verify. Researchers from Microsoft FORGE Lab checked every remaining finding by hand.

- Report privately. Reports reached maintainers through GitHub private vulnerability reporting, with a proof of concept and a suggested fix.

- Fix. Maintainers decided what to fix, how to fix it, and when.

Reports and fixes stayed on GitHub, where maintainers already work.

The result: Codename MDASH, using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model, flagged thousands of possible issues across the six projects. After AI triage and hand review by seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers, maintainers received 99 private reports. As of November 15, they had fixed 55, and 14 of those fixes were already in a release.

Participating projects

Six projects took part, all alumni of the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund. Their maintainers agreed to the scan, received every report privately, decided what to fix, and shared what worked:

- AutoGPT, an AI agent platform

- Caddy, a web server

- Express, a web framework for Node.js

- FastMCP, a framework for building MCP servers

- ImageMagick, image processing software

- Netty, a networking framework for Java

What we learned

These lessons come from what the six projects fixed and what their maintainers chose to share. Six projects is a small sample, so read them as early lessons.

1. Fixes matter more than findings

Fixing is where maintainers spend their time. So every report arrived already checked, with a suggested fix to review, adapt, and merge. Maintainers started from a well-scoped patch, not a raw finding.

The first fixes shipped about a week after the initial scan. Caddy’s maintainers fixed all 22 of the reports they received in a week or less. Maintainers used the suggested fixes, some as written and some with changes.

AutoGPT’s maintainers had recently shipped a new check, and it was broken. The report landed three days later and pointed at the right line. They took the fix further than the suggested patch, wrote it within a day, and had it in production less than a week later.

Finding vulnerabilities is no longer our bottleneck. Fixing them is the hard part, and that depends on maintainers.

Netty maintainer

2. Codename MDASH, with researcher review, gave maintainers high-quality findings with fixes

Maintainers got a short list, not a flood. Express maintainers said the reports cut through the noise. Caddy maintainers said they surfaced obscure bugs and filled gaps that earlier reports had missed. For FastMCP, the scan went beyond what AI scanners had given them before. ImageMagick, maintained by a two-person team, received 22 reports.

links.text: AI defending open source has to be better than the AI attacking it

items.title: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices
items.lede: Discover how we built the open Agent Host Protocol to keep your agent sessions accessible across editors, apps, phones, and the cloud.
items.text:
Models are now good enough to work for hours or even days on their own. You don’t have to watch over every thing they do, but you still need to be able to check in, no matter where you are. An agent can’t live only inside one application. The work should continue even If you close a window or switch devices.

In GitHub Copilot you can start an agent session in one place and pick it up in another. This session continuity runs on the Agent Host Protocol (AHP), an open standard built first in VS Code and adopted across GitHub. Here’s how it works, what we learned building it, and how you can use it to bring your agents into your own apps and workflows.

Why one integration per client stopped working

GitHub Copilot was first built in VS Code as an extension that bundled its own harness. This gave you access to your agents in VS Code, but it tied their lifetime to the editor. Extensions are attached to a single VS Code window. Close that window, and the agent is gone. Update VS Code, and every agent stops as the application restarts. Connect to a remote machine, and you get an entirely new extension host commit-locked against the version of the VS Code workbench you have.

At the same time, the Copilot app was being developed, alongside the existing GitHub mobile apps for iOS and Android. Each product was doing its own distinct integration with cloud-based agents to work towards delivering session continuity.

Each of these integrations solved the problem for one product, but developers also still want to be able to pull their agents into their own workflows–whether that’s an editor, a terminal, a phone, or a tool they built themselves–and they can’t do that if every client needs its own one-off integration. That’s why developers needed a protocol: a standard, independently versioned language across versions of VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, mobile apps, and any other client that might host an agent. A shared protocol means every client sees the same agents, history, and state without bespoke integrations, and you aren’t tied to one app’s idea of what an agent session is.

Designing a protocol for agents on every client

The protocol needed to allow multiple clients to interact with the same set of agents seamlessly. Start a session in the cloud from your phone, for example, then continue it from your laptop. It should tolerate network interruptions, reconnections, and concurrent client mutations. And it needed to be full-featured enough for you to do real work from each of your clients.

At the same time, the protocol needed to stay out of agent behavior. Unlike the domains that produced the Language Server Protocol and Debug Adapter Protocol, the world of agents is evolving quickly. That’s why AHP avoids encoding how agents work, and instead focuses on how you want to interact with them.

You also need the protocol to be simple enough to implement on your own client or server. While the full feature set would necessarily be extensive, the core protocol needed to be minimal.

The result of these requirements is the Agent Host Protocol (AHP). It is oriented around URI-identified “channels”, which are the coarsest unit of functionality in the protocol. Every server must implement the root, session, and chat channels, but can also implement more channels that provide terminal support, MCP additions, or OTel reporting, for example.

Within each channel is a reducer-based state object, which drives most of the logic for clients. The server is the arbiter of the state, and each client sends a sequence of actions that either mutate the state or trigger side effects, like sending a chat message. This provides a few very nice properties. Reconnection and replay in poor network conditions are easy: a client sends all queued actions, presents the right ‘loading’ state, and waits for the server to reconcile and acknowledge the actions before confirming them. Clients and servers are straightforward to debug. And reducer-based state also plays nicely with popular UI frameworks like React.

Shipping five clients and two hosts

Adopting the Agent Host Protocol in VS Code required building a new harness and agentic stack underneath it.
